# Consumer Ecommerce Support

`customer_support.model.b2c.ecommerce` · vertical · parent `customer_support.model.b2c`

> Supporting consumers who bought a physical thing online. Almost nothing in this queue is a question about how the product works; it is a question about where an order is, what state it arrived in, and whether the money is coming back. That changes the shape of the work in three ways. Resolution transfers value, not information. Refunds, replacements, credits and goodwill are the agent's actual toolkit, which means cost-to-serve includes the goods and not just the minutes, and an agent's authority limit is a real operating parameter. It also means resolutions are not reversible: a software answer given wrongly can be corrected, a dispatched replacement cannot be un-shipped. The facts belong to a carrier. For the largest single intent — where is my order — the truth is in a tracking system we do not control and cannot correct, so a large fraction of the queue is us relaying somebody else's information to an increasingly annoyed person while holding the liability. Generosity is farmed. The policy that resolves an honest customer in one message is the same policy an organised abuser runs at scale, so the tension between resolution speed and abuse control is permanent and cannot be settled by picking one. The error carried in from streaming or gaming is treating resolution as information delivery. The error carried in from B2B is investigating: at this volume, on this basket value, a fifteen-minute investigation to avoid a small refund is a loss, and the operator who cannot make that trade quickly clogs the queue behind them.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | the consumer who placed the order, or the recipient who did not — gifts and household orders routinely mean the person contacting us is not on the account |
| typical_resolution_hours | 6 |
| volume_shape | very high volume tracking order volume with a lag, spiking through promotional events and peak season and again two to three weeks later when returns land |
| staffing_model | pooled agents on shared queues with separate fraud/chargeback and returns pods, heavy seasonal contractor use |
| coverage | extended hours seven days, with chat and messaging carrying most of the interaction |
| automation_level | very high — order status, tracking and returns initiation are the most deflectable intents in the whole domain, and the economics assume they are deflected |
| notes | The returns wave is a second peak most staffing models forget. It arrives after the trading peak has been declared survived and it is staffed by whoever is left.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `intent_ref`, `resolution_type`


> Resolution type has to distinguish refund, replacement, credit, return-authorised and information-only, because those five have different cost, different reversibility and completely different abuse profiles. A queue that records them all as "resolved" can report excellent performance while giving away the margin.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `is_affected_user`


> Gift and household orders break the assumption that the contacting person is the buyer. The recipient has the problem and the buyer has the account, the payment method and the refund right — and an agent who resolves with whoever wrote in has created a dispute with someone who has not spoken yet.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.customer_sentiment`

Requires `public_exposure`


> Anger here is cheap to broadcast and expensive to receive. A marketplace review, a chargeback and a social post are all one click away, and the same reading of frustration justifies a faster and more generous response than it would in B2B — not because the customer is angrier, but because the alternative channel is worse for us.
